title: How A One-Second Strategy Can Motivate Your New Class
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin describes a small ritual he's used for years: a homemade poster reading 'Learn Like A Champion Today' that students tap on their way into the classroom, inspired by a similar tradition at Notre Dame and Oklahoma football. He explains that the poster's power lies not in the object itself but in the meaning students assign to the act — an entirely voluntary physical commitment to give their best, behave their best, and maintain a positive attitude. Crucially, Linsin insists the ritual must remain completely optional; forcing or glaring at students who skip it destroys its power. He notes the strategy tends to be more, not less, effective at more challenging schools, provided students already enjoy being part of the class. The piece frames the poster as a small but meaningful daily reset that reinforces responsibility and culture without requiring any real-time enforcement.
points: A simple physical ritual — tapping a poster before entering class — can function as a voluntary daily commitment device when its meaning is explicitly taught beforehand.
The ritual's power comes entirely from the meaning students assign to it, not the object itself; it must be introduced and modeled during the first week of school.
The tap represents three specific voluntary commitments: to give their best, behave their best, and have a positive attitude — not formal rules.
The ritual must remain entirely optional; forcing participation or reacting negatively when students skip it destroys its effectiveness.
The strategy tends to be more, not less, effective at challenging schools, provided students already enjoy being part of the classroom culture.
quotes: For years I’ve had a poster on my classroom door that reads “Learn Like A Champion Today.” Each student taps it on their way in.
But the act of tapping it, the decision to reach up and give it a rap, is where you’ll find its power. It’s the meaning behind the action that makes it work.
You must walk your students outside your classroom during the first week of school and, while modeling how you want them to enter, explain that by tapping the poster they're agreeing to three things.
Because it must be entirely their choice. If it isn’t, if you force your students to tap it or glare at them when they don’t, then it loses its power. It no longer possesses any meaning.
In fact, the more challenging the school, the more impactful the strategy.
It's a strategy that helps ensure that each day begins on the right foot, that each day starts with a reminder that entering your classroom comes with responsibility.
